shorts.name: SubmarineOtherGas
shorts.title: The Other Gas a Submarine Has to Fight

lines.text: Seal a hundred and forty-five people in a steel tube, and the air goes bad in two separate ways — and making oxygen only fixes one of them.
The other is carbon dioxide — and the biggest source on board is the crew's own breath.
So air is pushed through a scrubber containing an amine, which grabs carbon dioxide. Heat it, and the gas is released and pumped out of the boat.
Even then, it's never zero: in data reported in 2003, US nuclear submarines averaged several times the carbon dioxide of outdoor air.
That's why a submarine needs two machines for its air: one to make oxygen, and one to pull carbon dioxide back out.

shorts.name: SubmarineNoGPS
shorts.title: How a Submarine Knows Where It Is With No GPS

lines.text: Once a submarine dives, GPS is gone.
GPS works by radio, and seawater soaks up radio — its signals can't reach a submerged submarine.
So the boat keeps track of itself. Gyroscopes sense every turn, accelerometers sense every push and pull, and a computer adds it all up.
The catch: tiny errors add up too, and the estimate slowly drifts.
So every so often it checks against something outside — for example, coming up near the surface for a GPS fix, or matching the seafloor below to a map. Methods vary between navies and boats.
Sense the motion, add it up, then check it — that's how a submarine finds its way without GPS.

shorts.name: SubmarineMessages
shorts.title: How Do You Send a Message to a Hidden Submarine?

lines.text: Seawater soaks up radio — so how does a hidden submarine get a message?
The higher the frequency, the faster it disappears. Very-low-frequency radio gets in — but, according to the US Navy, only tens of feet.
So to listen, a submarine has to get an antenna up near the surface — which limits how deep and fast it can go, and makes it easier to spot.
The US also ran an extremely-low-frequency system, at about 76 hertz, that reached submarines hundreds of feet down — but only one way, slowly. It was shut down in 2004.
So every message to a hidden submarine is a trade: to hear it, the boat gives up some depth, speed or stealth.

shorts.name: SubmarineOxygen
shorts.title: How Submarines Make Air Out of Water

lines.text: A nuclear submarine makes its own oxygen — by splitting water.
An electrolyser runs electric current through water and splits it into oxygen and hydrogen.
The oxygen goes into the air. The hydrogen is explosive in enough quantity, so on US submarines it's sent out of the boat, into the sea.
And oxygen is held close to normal air: too little dulls thinking, too much makes fires more dangerous.
Water and electricity — that's how a nuclear submarine makes the oxygen its crew breathes.

shorts.name: SubmarinePressureHull
shorts.title: What Holds Back the Ocean on a Submarine

lines.text: Every ten metres of seawater adds roughly another atmosphere of pressure.
So the part of a submarine that holds the sea back — the pressure hull — is a round steel tube, braced by rings of steel frames.
Engineers design it so the shell can't buckle inward or crumple.
How deep real submarines go isn't published — but at any depth, it's that ring-braced steel tube holding the sea back.

shorts.name: SubmarineStealth
shorts.title: How Do You Hide Something the Length of a Football Field Underwater?

lines.text: A US Virginia-class submarine is three hundred and seventy-seven feet long — about the length of a football field. So how does something that big stay hidden underwater?
Water carries sound remarkably well. Low-frequency sound loses very little energy to absorption, so low rumbles can be detected a long way off; higher-pitched sounds fade much sooner.
Many submarines are wrapped in special coatings. Some soak up incoming sonar pings, so less sound echoes back. Others muffle the noise the boat itself makes.
It doesn't make a submarine silent. It makes it harder to hear — and harder to find.

shorts.name: SubmarineEnduranceLimits
shorts.title: What Actually Limits How Long a Nuclear Sub Stays Down?

lines.text: A nuclear submarine cleans its own air, and today's reactor cores are rated for over a million miles — so why does it ever come home?
Unlike surface warships, submarines are almost never resupplied at sea. Everything the crew will eat is loaded before they leave.
Crews and machines need time ashore too: US ballistic-missile submarines average 77 days at sea, then 35 in port for maintenance, with two crews taking turns.
Food, maintenance, the people aboard and the mission — those set the clock.
